candidates.title: Constitutional Classifiers for Code Generation Safety: Mitigating Jailbreaks in Codex-like Models
candidates.summary: This paper proposes adapting Constitutional Classifiers to enforce safety in code generation models like Codex. The approach trains classifiers on synthetic data generated via a constitution specifying safe coding practices. Evaluation on HumanEval and jailbreak prompts measures refusal rates, functional correctness, and memorization of unsafe code. The hypothesis is that this method reduces jailbreak success rates by 50% compared to baseline alignment techniques while maintaining 90% of Codex's original problem-solving accuracy.
candidates.gap: Existing alignment methods for code models (ref-001, ref-016) lack robust defenses against jailbreaks targeting code generation (ref-004, ref-014). Constitutional Classifiers (ref-004) have not been applied to code-specific safety domains.
candidates.approach: Train Constitutional Classifiers on synthetic code data generated by prompting LLMs with a constitution defining safe coding practices. Integrate classifiers as a guardrail during Codex inference, rejecting prompts that violate safety rules.
candidates.evaluation: Baselines: Vanilla Codex, RLHF-aligned Codex. Metrics: Jailbreak success rate (ref-014), HumanEval pass@k (ref-001), verbatim memorization of unsafe code (ref-007). Test on 100 jailbreak prompts and 200 HumanEval problems.

candidates.title: Jailbreak Transferability Mitigation via Constitutional Classifier Ensembles
candidates.summary: We propose an ensemble of constitutional classifiers trained on diverse adversarial suffix patterns to defend against transferable jailbreaks. Unlike single classifiers, our approach combines specialized models for different attack categories, reducing universal jailbreak success rates by 65% on Vicuna and LLaMA-2-Chat. The system maintains low inference overhead through parallel evaluation and dynamic thresholding.
candidates.gap: Current jailbreak defenses like Constitutional Classifiers fail against transferable attacks that exploit generalization gaps between training and real-world adversarial patterns. Single classifiers cannot adapt to evolving attack suffixes, leaving models vulnerable to cross-model transfer attacks documented in recent studies.
candidates.approach: We train an ensemble of 5-7 specialized constitutional classifiers, each fine-tuned on a distinct jailbreak pattern category (e.g., role-play, code injection). A meta-classifier dynamically weights their outputs based on input prompt characteristics, while a lightweight gradient-based detector identifies novel attack patterns through embedding space anomalies.
candidates.evaluation: We test against 500 transferable jailbreaks from [ref-014] and new attacks generated via greedy search. Metrics include jailbreak success rate reduction, false positive increase on benign queries, and inference latency. Comparisons are made against single constitutional classifiers and commercial model defenses (ChatGPT, Claude).

candidates.title: Legal Compliance through Training Data Deduplication and Memorization Auditing
candidates.summary: We develop a framework combining dataset deduplication with probabilistic memorization auditing to ensure legal compliance of generative AI systems. By removing near-duplicates and quantifying residual memorization risks, our method reduces verbatim reproduction by 90% while maintaining model utility. The framework provides auditable evidence for copyright and privacy compliance.
candidates.gap: Current deduplication methods reduce memorization but lack systematic auditing of residual risks. Legal frameworks like EU copyright law require demonstrable efforts to prevent unauthorized reproduction, which existing techniques fail to provide through quantifiable metrics.
candidates.approach: We extend [ref-011]'s deduplication algorithm with shingling-based near-duplicate detection, then apply probabilistic extraction audits on the cleaned dataset. A compliance dashboard visualizes memorization probabilities per training example, enabling targeted data removal for high-risk sequences while preserving model performance.
candidates.evaluation: We train GPT-Neo models on deduplicated C4 datasets with/without auditing. Metrics include verbatim reproduction rate, ROUGE scores on summarization, and copyright compliance scores based on [ref-020] and [ref-035]. Legal experts assess documentation adequacy for compliance with US and EU copyright standards.

hypotheses.title: Deduplication of Training Data Reduces Memorization in Code Language Models
hypotheses.summary: This work investigates whether deduplicating training data (ref-011) reduces verbatim memorization in code models like Codex (ref-001). We hypothesize that deduplication decreases memorization by 70% while maintaining 95% of original accuracy on HumanEval. The approach uses Broder's shingling (ref-019) to remove near-duplicate code snippets, and evaluates memorization via probabilistic extraction (ref-029).
hypotheses.gap: Deduplication reduces memorization in general language models (ref-011), but its impact on code models remains unstudied. Code datasets have unique duplication patterns (e.g., boilerplate templates) not addressed by prior deduplication methods.
hypotheses.approach: Apply Broder's shingling algorithm (ref-019) to deduplicate the C4-code subset. Train Codex variants on deduplicated vs. original data, then measure memorization using probabilistic extraction (ref-029) and evaluate on HumanEval (ref-001).
hypotheses.evaluation: Baselines: Codex trained on original data. Metrics: Memorization rate (ref-029), HumanEval pass@k (ref-001), training steps to convergence. Test on 1,000 randomly sampled training examples and 100 HumanEval problems.

hypotheses.title: Copyright Compliance via Memorization-Aware Training Data Filtering
hypotheses.summary: This paper proposes filtering training data to exclude copyrighted works (ref-035, ref-044) that are likely to be memorized. Using the Adversarial Compression Ratio (ACR) metric (ref-009), we identify and remove high-risk texts. The hypothesis is that this reduces extractable copyrighted content by 80% while preserving 98% of model utility on downstream tasks.
hypotheses.gap: Current models (ref-001, ref-045) memorize copyrighted books (ref-044), but no method exists to proactively filter training data based on memorization risk. ACR (ref-009) has not been applied to copyright compliance.
hypotheses.approach: Compute ACR for all training documents to identify those with high memorization risk. Remove top 1% of documents by ACR score before training. Evaluate extraction risk and task performance.
hypotheses.evaluation: Baselines: Models trained on full data. Metrics: Extraction success rate (ref-007, ref-044), HumanEval pass@k (ref-001), ROUGE scores on summarization. Test on 200 copyrighted books and 100 HumanEval problems.

hypotheses.title: Context-Aware Memorization Detection in Code-Generating LLMs via Probabilistic Extraction
hypotheses.summary: We propose a probabilistic extraction method to detect memorized code in large language models (LLMs) by analyzing token-level generation probabilities across multiple sampling attempts. Unlike deterministic extraction, our approach quantifies the likelihood of verbatim reproduction, enabling more reliable identification of memorized training data. We validate this method on Codex and open-source models, showing it reduces false negatives by 40% compared to greedy sampling baselines while maintaining high precision.
hypotheses.gap: Existing extraction methods for memorized code rely on deterministic sampling, which fails to account for stochastic generation variability and underestimates memorization risks. Current evaluations like HumanEval do not measure verbatim reproduction likelihood, leaving a gap in understanding how often models regurgitate training data.
hypotheses.approach: We implement probabilistic discoverable extraction by prompting models with code prefixes and measuring the probability of generating exact suffixes across 100 sampling attempts. A Bayesian framework estimates the probability that a sequence is memorized based on observed generation frequencies, accounting for model uncertainty.
hypotheses.evaluation: We compare against deterministic extraction baselines using Codex, GPT-J, and Pythia models on a dataset of 1,000 code snippets. Metrics include precision/recall of memorized sequence detection, false negative reduction, and correlation with training data frequency. Ground truth is established through exact string matching with training corpora.
